title: Gimel runs to dalet (Shabbat 104a)
hookLine: the rabbis say gimel's foot runs after dalet: the giver chases the poor

lines: CHILDREN IN THE HOUSE OF STUDY.
cards: The Talmud tells of a classroom turned upside down. Some young children walk into the house of study, where the rabbis sit with their books, and start teaching. Not reciting.
Teaching. They go through the alphabet letter by letter, explaining what each one is saying, and the rabbis write it down, impressed enough to say nothing like it had been heard in a very long time.
At the third and fourth letters, gimel and dalet, the children point at something tiny in how the letters are drawn. A foot.

teach.h: GEMOL DALIM: BE KIND TO THE POOR.
teach.b: First, the two letters as a phrase. The children read gimel dalet as gemol dalim: be kind to the poor. Gimel stands for the giver, dalet for the one in need.
Gimel is drawn with a little leg reaching out at the bottom, toward dalet. Why? Because, the children say, it's the way of someone who does kindness to run after the poor.
Not to sit at home and wait for a knock. To go looking. Third, dalet's answer.
Dalet has a leg of its own, reaching back toward gimel, so the poor person makes themselves available to be found.
But dalet's face is turned away from gimel, so the gift is given in secret, and the one receiving it isn't ashamed. Run toward the need, then look away while it's met. Fourth, the giving itself.
Giving only when asked, or only when seen, asks little.

These two letters ask something harder: notice the need before anyone has to say it, close the distance yourself, and protect the other person's dignity, so what they remember is the help, not the embarrassment.
The children in the study house found all of that in a foot and a turned face.

how: Jewish teaching on tzedakah, giving to those in need, prizes giving that seeks out the need and spares the receiver shame; the Talmud reads this into the shapes of gimel and dalet.

games.q: what does “gimel runs to dalet” mean?
o: the giver running after the poor, and giving quietly
the poor chasing the rich for a share of their wealth
two letters that always appear side by side

games.q: gimel runs to dalet — tap the pairs.

s: in this Talmud story, the rabbis teach the children the alphabet
it's the other way round: young children come into the house of study and teach the rabbis.
the children say dalet faces away so the gift is given in secret
so the one who receives is not ashamed.
gimel's foot is read as the giver waiting to be asked
it runs after the poor: the giver goes looking.

games.q: you've noticed a neighbor is struggling. nobody has asked you for anything. by the reading of gimel and dalet, what do you do?
o: wait until they ask, so you don't intrude.
go toward the need, and give quietly.
give publicly, so others will follow.
games.why: gimel runs after dalet, and dalet's face is turned away: go looking for the need, and give in secret so no one is shamed.

practice: Bring to mind a need near you that nobody has asked you to meet: a neighbor stretched thin, a coworker short this month, a food bank down the road.

Hold it, and picture one gift you could give in a way that leaves nobody feeling watched, like groceries left at the door or a donation with no name on it. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Gimel runs to dalet. The Talmud's reading of two letters: gemol dalim, the giver running after the poor, and giving quietly. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: be kind to the poor, the Talmud's reading of gimel and dalet.

carryVoice: Your line: gimel runs to dalet. Kindness that runs doesn't wait for a knock. See you at dalet.
